title: Interval DP: Longest Palindromic Substring
oneLiner: Whether a whole SUBSTRING is a palindrome depends on whether the substring one character shorter, INSIDE it, already was -- the interval-DP shape: solve small ranges first, use them to answer bigger ranges.
keyTakeaway: isPalin(i, j) ("is s[i..j] a palindrome") is true exactly when the outer characters match (s[i] == s[j]) AND the INNER substring s[i+1..j-1] is also a palindrome -- so processing every substring in order of INCREASING LENGTH guarantees the shorter inner answer is already known by the time a longer interval needs it. This returns the LENGTH of the longest palindromic substring, not the substring itself, since more than one substring can tie for longest (e.g. "bab" and "aba" inside "babad") and only the length has one unambiguous right answer.
explanation:
Every DP concept so far in this app has built a 1-D array where each cell depends on one or two PRIOR cells. Interval DP is the same overlapping-subproblems idea applied to RANGES [i, j] of the input instead of single positions -- and the classic example is checking every substring of a string for whether it's a palindrome.

The recurrence: a substring s[i..j] is a palindrome if its outer characters match (s[i] == s[j]) AND everything INSIDE those two characters, s[i+1..j-1], is itself a palindrome. That inner check is a SMALLER interval -- so if every interval is processed in order of increasing LENGTH (all length-1 intervals first, then all length-2, then length-3, ...), the inner answer a longer interval needs has always already been computed. Every single character is trivially a palindrome of length 1 (the base case), and a 2-character interval is a palindrome exactly when its two characters match (no room for an inner check).

This is genuinely a different shape from the DP concepts before it: the STATE isn't "how far into the input am I" (a single index), it's "which interval [i, j] am I asking about" (two indices), and the processing ORDER (shortest intervals first) matters just as much as the recurrence itself -- checking a length-5 interval before its length-3 inner interval has been computed would read a stale or missing answer.

Watch the highlighted window below sweep every interval in increasing-length order, and the tracker update whenever a longer palindrome is found.

starterCode.python:
def longest_palindrome_length(s):
    # TODO: dp[i][j] = True if s[i..j] is a palindrome. Base cases: every single
    # character (length 1) is a palindrome; a 2-character range is a palindrome iff its
    # two characters match. For longer ranges: dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and dp[i+1][j-1].
    # Process ranges shortest-to-longest. Return the longest length found.
    return 1 if len(s) > 0 else 0

recognitionSignals: The problem is about a CONTIGUOUS range (substring, subarray) rather than a subsequence, and whether a range "works" depends on whether a SMALLER range strictly inside it also worked.
You catch yourself wanting to check every possible (i, j) pair -- that's the O(n^2) STATE space interval DP fills in, same way a 1-D dp array fills every index.
gotchas: Processing order matters here in a way it didn't for earlier DP concepts: intervals MUST be handled shortest-to-longest, or a longer interval's inner lookup reads a cell that hasn't been filled in yet.

The longest palindrome isn't always unique ("babad" has both "bab" and "aba" at length 3) -- this lesson deliberately asks for the LENGTH, not the substring itself, to sidestep that ambiguity entirely.
confusableWith: Dynamic Programming: Longest Increasing Subsequence (this track) is also "build up from smaller answers," but its state is a single index, not a two-index interval, and order doesn't matter beyond left-to-right.

complexity.note: There are ~n²/2 intervals [i, j], each filled in O(1) from a smaller interval; the dp table holds one cell per interval.
